# Triangulation

**The ceiling methods and the reachable method are NOT supposed to agree, and we refuse to average them. Their gap is the single most useful number here.**

| Scenario | M1 ceiling | M2 ceiling | Reachable | Ceiling span | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 168.8-196.4 cr | 139.7-838.5 cr | 1.8-15.8 cr | 6.0x | 53.0x |
| B | 1446.0-1682.5 cr | 1197.1-7182.7 cr | 15.1-135.6 cr | 6.0x | 53.0x |

## Rule applied

M1 and M2 are ceilings: they state what would exist if we won every eligible institution. The reachable method applies an explicit adoption-and-capture band. Report both. The ratio between them is the growth headroom an investor is buying.

## The two independent ceiling methods

M1 builds bottom-up from institution counts; M2 builds top-down from the India higher-education technology market. They share no inputs. They land within 6.0x of each other, which is within one order of magnitude - weak agreement, but genuine agreement, and materially better than the published alternative.

## Why we refuse to average

> Phase 5 recorded conflict C-05: two research houses size the SAME market 625x apart (US$499M vs US$0.8M). Published sizing in this category is demonstrably unusable. That is why M1 is built bottom-up from institution counts and budget documents rather than from a report.

Averaging M1, M2 and R would produce a single rupee figure sitting between a ceiling and a reachable estimate. That figure would mean nothing, would move whenever we changed the capture band, and would be impossible to falsify because it describes no particular claim.

## For the investor

> A TAM is a ceiling, not a forecast. The number to underwrite is SOM, which is capacity-built and roughly two orders of magnitude below TAM. Anyone showing one TAM number without its method is asking you to trust a method they have not shown you. Ours are all three, and one of them is the bad news.
